chunks: "There are really three layers. The lowest is commutation: figuring out which phases to energise based on rotor position.
Above that is modulation: PWM-ing the bridge so the average voltage is what I want. Above that are the regulation loops: a speed loop wrapped around a current loop.
The simplest method is six-step, or trapezoidal, control.
Three Hall sensors give me the sector, a lookup table picks which two phases conduct, and I PWM the high or low side to set the voltage.
Speed control is a PI loop on measured speed from the Hall edge timing, and I'd add a current limit using a shunt.
It's cheap and robust, but you get torque ripple at six times the electrical frequency, so it's audible and not great at low speed.
If there are no Hall sensors, I use sensorless control: watch the floating phase's back-EMF, detect the zero-crossing, and commutate 30 electrical degrees later.
It needs an open-loop startup and doesn't work at standstill. For smooth, efficient, quiet control I'd use field-oriented control.
I measure two phase currents, transform them with Clarke and Park into a rotating frame aligned with the rotor, and run PI loops on the d and q currents.
The q current gives torque directly, so torque control is clean, and I can drive sinusoidal phase currents.
It needs a good rotor angle, so an encoder or an observer, and more compute.
So I'd pick six-step for fans and pumps, FOC for robot joints, e-bikes and anything where smoothness and efficiency matter."
